item.title: Hiroshima Ramen & Tsukemen: The City's Noodle Bowls — Guide
item.description: Hiroshima has two distinct noodle traditions of its own. Hiroshima ramen is a relatively gentle, comforting bowl: a soy-based broth built on pork bones, less heavy than Hakata tonkotsu, with soft straight noodles, chashu pork, bean sprouts and spring onion. Quite different is Hiroshima tsukemen, a local speciality unrelated to the Tokyo dipping-noodle style: chilled noodles served with raw cabbage and cucumber alongside a cold, intensely spicy chilli-and-sesame dipping sauce, ordered by heat level from mild to genuinely punishing.

item.title: Mamakari: Okayama's Vinegar-Pickled Little Fish — Guide
item.description: Mamakari is a small silvery fish of the Seto Inland Sea, a kind of sardine or shad, and one of Okayama’s most characteristic foods. It is usually filleted and cured in vinegar, giving a bright, sharp, oily bite eaten as sashimi-style sushi, with rice, or as a drinking snack. The name is a local joke: mama means cooked rice and kari means to borrow, because the fish is so good with rice that you finish your own bowl and have to borrow more from the neighbours.

item.title: Nara Persimmons: Kaki, Dried Fruit and Leaf-Wrapped Sushi — Guide
item.description: Nara is one of Japan’s foremost producers of kaki (persimmon), its warm valleys — especially around Gojo and the Yoshino foothills — filled with orchards that turn brilliant orange each autumn. The fruit runs deep in local culture: eaten fresh and crisp in autumn, slowly air-dried into intensely sweet, chewy hoshigaki (dried persimmon) hung in curtains under the eaves, worked into wagashi and jams, and even its leaves are used to wrap the region’s famous kakinoha-zushi.

item.title: Gunma Wagyu & Yakiniku: Premium Grilled Beef from the Mountains — Guide
item.description: Gunma produces several respected wagyu beef brands, including Jomo Wagyu, raised on the prefecture’s cool mountain pastures under careful breeding and feeding standards that produce fine, even marbling and a rich, tender flavour. The beef is served throughout Gunma in dedicated yakiniku (grilled meat) restaurants, where diners grill thin-cut slices themselves at the table, as well as in steakhouses and traditional sukiyaki and shabu-shabu preparations, offering visitors an accessible taste of high-grade Japanese beef outside the more famous Kobe and Matsusaka brands.

item.title: Hegi Soba: Seaweed-Bound Buckwheat Noodles, Elegantly Plated — Guide
item.description: Hegi soba is a distinctive Niigata noodle tradition, its buckwheat noodles bound with funori, a type of edible seaweed, rather than the egg typically used elsewhere in Japan, giving the noodles a notably smooth, glossy texture and slight chewiness. The dish takes its name from the wooden hegi tray it’s traditionally served on, with the noodles arranged in elegant, bite-sized folds (tsumami) rather than a simple pile, making it both a distinctive regional specialty and a visually memorable dining experience.

item.title: Hitachi Beef: Ibaraki's Premium Wagyu — Guide
item.description: Hitachi beef (Hitachi-gyu) is Ibaraki’s premium wagyu brand, raised on the prefecture’s rich pastureland under strict quality standards that govern feed, breeding and grading. Known for its fine, even marbling and tender texture, the beef is served across the prefecture in dedicated steakhouses, yakiniku grill restaurants and traditional sukiyaki and shabu-shabu establishments, offering a genuine taste of high-grade Japanese wagyu outside the more famous Kobe or Matsusaka brands. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Various towns across Ibaraki Hours Lunch & dinner, restaurant-dependent Admission Set meals typically ¥3,000–8,000+ Time needed 1–1.

item.title: Kuji Chicken (Okukuji Shamo): Free-Range Flavour from the Mountains — Guide
item.description: Kuji chicken, more formally known as Okukuji Shamo, is a heritage chicken breed raised free-range in the mountainous Okukuji region of northern Ibaraki, prized for a firmer texture and richer flavour than mass-produced broiler chicken. The breed’s slower growth and active outdoor rearing produce meat favoured by chefs for yakitori skewers, hot pot and other preparations where the chicken’s distinct character can shine, and it appears in regional bento boxes sold at local train stations.

item.title: Kusatsu Onsen Manju: Steamed Buns Cooked with Hot Spring Vapour — Guide
item.description: Onsen manju, sweet steamed buns filled with red bean paste, are a beloved snack found across Japan’s hot spring towns, but Kusatsu’s version carries a particular local charm — traditionally, some shops cooked the buns using steam vented directly from the town’s natural hot springs rather than conventional kitchen equipment. Dozens of shops around the Yubatake sell warm, freshly steamed manju, each with slight variations in dough colour, sweetness, and bean paste texture, making a comparison tasting a popular activity for visitors strolling the town.

item.title: Mito Natto: Japan's Fermented Soybean Capital — Guide
item.description: Mito is Japan’s most famous natto-producing region, so closely associated with the sticky, pungent fermented soybean dish that the city’s name has become a byword for it nationwide. The tradition is said to date back centuries, and today dozens of manufacturers across the city continue the craft, several offering factory tours that walk visitors through the fermentation process, from steaming soybeans to the addition of natto bacteria, followed by tastings of various grades and bean sizes.

item.title: Mizusawa Udon: One of Japan's Three Great Udon Styles — Guide
item.description: Mizusawa udon, ranked among Japan’s three great regional udon styles, is produced in the small area around Mizusawa Kannon temple near Ikaho, its silky, elastic hand-pulled noodles owing their exceptional texture to pure spring water sourced from the base of nearby Mount Haruna. Dozens of specialist restaurants cluster around the temple approach, most serving the noodles simply — cold, with a light dipping sauce — allowing the noodles' clean flavour and springy bite to take centre stage.

item.title: Nikko & Nasu Soba: Handmade Buckwheat Noodles from Tochigi's Highlands — Guide
item.description: Tochigi’s cool mountain climate and well-drained highland soil, particularly around Nikko and Nasu, are ideal for growing high-quality buckwheat, making the prefecture a respected soba noodle region. Specialist shops, some with dedicated buckwheat fields visible from the dining room, prepare noodles by hand from freshly milled flour, served either cold with a dipping sauce (zaru soba) or hot in broth, with a firm bite and pronounced buckwheat aroma that distinguishes handmade soba from mass-produced versions.

item.title: Nikko Onsen Town Kaiseki: A Multi-Course Feast After the Bath — Guide
item.description: Kaiseki, Japan’s traditional multi-course haute cuisine, is served each evening at ryokan across Nikko’s onsen towns, following a customary post-bath dinner tradition that transforms a simple hot spring stay into a full culinary experience. Nikko’s kaiseki menus typically showcase the region’s signature ingredients — delicate yuba tofu skin, foraged mountain vegetables (sansai), and river fish such as trout — presented across a carefully sequenced series of small, artfully arranged courses that change with the seasons.

item.title: Nikko Yuba: Delicate Tofu Skin, a Temple-Town Specialty — Guide
item.description: Yuba, the delicate skin that forms on the surface of simmering soy milk, has been a Nikko speciality since the town’s temples adopted it centuries ago as a protein-rich substitute within Buddhist vegetarian cuisine. Nikko’s exceptionally pure mountain water is credited with producing a particularly fine, flavourful yuba, and today dozens of restaurants and shops across the town serve it in countless preparations — as delicate sashimi-style slices, deep-fried, simmered in broth, or wrapped around other ingredients.

item.title: Noppe: Niigata's Comforting Root Vegetable Stew — Guide
item.description: Noppe (or noppei-jiru) is a traditional Niigata comfort dish, a gently simmered stew combining root vegetables like taro and carrot with mushrooms, konjac and often seafood such as salmon or scallop, bound in a light, slightly thickened broth. The dish varies considerably from household to household and season to season, but it holds a special place in Niigata’s New Year celebrations, when it’s traditionally prepared in larger batches and served slightly cool, its comforting simplicity representing a homely counterpoint to the region’s more elaborate seafood and sake specialities.

item.title: Tarekatsu-don: Niigata's Sauce-Glazed Take on Katsudon — Guide
item.description: Tarekatsu-don is Niigata’s distinctive regional take on katsudon (pork cutlet rice bowl), diverging from the egg-simmered version common across most of Japan by instead dipping a freshly fried, crisp pork cutlet into a sweet-savoury soy-based sauce (tare) and laying it directly over a bed of plain rice, without egg. The result keeps the cutlet’s crispy exterior intact rather than softening it in simmered egg, giving Niigata’s version a satisfying textural contrast between the crunchy pork and soft rice beneath.

item.title: Kawagoe Sweet Potato Snacks: Little Edo's Signature Treat — Guide
item.description: Kawagoe has been famous for its sweet potatoes (satsumaimo) since the Edo period, when the region’s rich volcanic ash soil proved ideal for cultivation, supplying the growing city of Edo with a reliable food source. Today the historic streets are lined with shops transforming the humble sweet potato into an astonishing variety of treats — roasted whole (yaki-imo), baked into tarts and cakes, blended into soft-serve ice cream, or fried into crisp chips, making it one of Kawagoe’s most recognisable culinary identities.

item.title: Kitakata Ramen: One of Japan's Three Great Ramen Styles — Guide
item.description: Kitakata ramen is ranked among Japan’s three great regional ramen styles, distinguished by thick, wavy, hand-cut noodles in a light, clear soy-and-pork (shoyu) broth. The small city of Kitakata, with a population of roughly 30,000, is home to more than 100 ramen shops — reportedly the highest ramen-shop density per capita in Japan — many of them family-run for generations, and locals famously eat it for breakfast (asa-ramen) as often as lunch or dinner.

item.title: Musashino Udon: Firm, Dark-Broth Noodles of the Saitama Plain — Guide
item.description: Musashino udon is a distinctive regional noodle style native to the Musashino plateau spanning Saitama and western Tokyo, characterised by notably firm, chewy, hand-cut noodles served separately from a rich, dark, soy-based dipping broth (tsukejiru) often studded with pork and vegetables. The style developed from the region’s historical wheat cultivation, an alternative to rice farming on the plateau’s drier soil, and remains a point of local pride, with dedicated shops throughout Saitama each guarding their own broth recipe.

item.title: Saitama Unagi: Grilled Eel Over Rice, a Landlocked Speciality — Guide
item.description: Grilled eel over rice (unaju or unadon) is a beloved Saitama speciality, a somewhat unexpected tradition for a landlocked prefecture that developed thanks to the abundant rivers historically stocked with freshwater eel and the region’s role supplying Edo (old Tokyo) with food. Specialist unagi restaurants, some family-run for generations, prepare the eel with a meticulous process of steaming and charcoal-grilling with a sweet-savoury glaze, resulting in a dish that’s crisp outside and meltingly tender within.

item.title: Sasa Kamaboko: Sendai's Bamboo-Leaf-Shaped Fish Cake — Guide
item.description: Sasa kamaboko is a Sendai speciality — a grilled fish cake made from white fish paste, shaped like a bamboo leaf (sasa) and hand-fanned into its distinctive form before grilling over an open flame. It was created over a century ago as a way to preserve the abundant white fish catches of Miyagi’s coast, and remains a beloved snack and souvenir, with a smoky exterior and springy, delicately sweet interior.

item.title: Sendai Gyutan: Grilled Beef Tongue, Miyagi's Signature Dish — Guide
item.description: Grilled beef tongue (gyutan) is Sendai’s culinary trademark — thick slices of ox tongue, salted and aged, then char-grilled over binchotan charcoal until the edges crisp while the centre stays tender. The dish was invented after WWII by a Sendai restaurateur who didn’t want to waste tongue meat discarded by US military kitchens, and has since become the city’s signature, served in dozens of specialist restaurants around Sendai Station. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Sendai, Miyagi Hours Lunch & dinner, most restaurants Admission Set meals from ~¥1,500 Time needed About 1 hour Best time Year-round What to Try The classic gyutan teishoku (grilled tongue set with oxtail soup, barley rice, pickles).

item.title: Sendai Miso: A Bold Red Miso with Samurai Roots — Guide
item.description: Sendai miso is a distinctive dark red, unpasteurised soybean paste with a bold, slightly bitter depth of flavour, aged for over a year in wooden vats. Its origins trace to the early 1600s, when warlord Date Masamune established a dedicated miso brewery to supply his troops with long-lasting, nutritious rations — making it one of Japan’s oldest continuously produced regional misos. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Sendai, Miyagi Hours Shop hours; some breweries offer tours Admission Free tasting at many shops; miso from ~¥500 Time needed 30–45 min Best time Year-round What to Try Rich miso soup made with Sendai miso at local restaurants.

item.title: Zunda Mochi: Sendai's Vivid Green Edamame Sweet — Guide
item.description: Zunda mochi is one of Sendai’s most distinctive sweets — soft rice cakes coated in a vividly green paste of mashed young soybeans (edamame), sweetened and lightly salted. The dish is said to date back to the samurai era, when warlord Date Masamune’s troops reportedly mashed beans with sword hilts during a campaign. Today it’s sold everywhere from department store basements to Sendai Station kiosks, as mochi, shakes, and even soft-serve ice cream.

item.title: Chiba Peanuts Guide: Japan's Top Peanuts, Sweets & Where to Buy
item.description: Chiba is Japan’s peanut capital, producing the lion’s share of the country’s domestic crop — and “Chiba peanuts” are a prized, premium souvenir nationwide. The sandy soils around Yachimata and the Boso interior yield famously sweet, fragrant nuts that locals enjoy in every form: freshly boiled (yude-rakkasei) in autumn, classic roasted, ground into nutty peanut confections, and even as peanut soft-serve ice cream. From specialty shops and roadside stands to elegant gift boxes, peanuts here are a genuine regional craft.

item.title: Jingisukan Guide: Hokkaido's Grilled Lamb BBQ & Where to Eat
item.description: Jingisukan (“Genghis Khan”) is Hokkaido’s beloved grilled-mutton barbecue, a smoky, sociable feast named for the dome-shaped grill said to resemble a warrior’s helmet. Diners cook lamb or mutton and a pile of vegetables — onions, beansprouts, cabbage, pumpkin — over the convex iron grill, where juices run down to flavour the veg around the rim. Washed down with ice-cold beer in a summer beer garden or a lively grill house, it’s one of Hokkaido’s most fun and convivial meals.

item.title: Odawara Kamaboko & Seafood Guide: What to Eat & Access
item.description: The castle town of Odawara, gateway to Hakone, is one of Japan’s great homes of kamaboko — the springy steamed fish cake refined here over centuries thanks to fresh Sagami Bay catch and clean mountain water. Beyond the famous pink-and-white loaves, Odawara serves up fresh fish, grilled age-kama fritters, and a lively port market. Visitors can tour kamaboko makers, taste the difference between artisan and everyday versions, and even make their own at hands-on workshops.

item.title: Okinawan Cuisine Guide: Goya Champuru, Rafute & More
item.description: Okinawan cuisine is a world of its own — shaped by the Ryukyu Kingdom, Chinese and Southeast Asian trade, and a famous longevity food culture. Its signature dish is goya champuru, a stir-fry of bitter melon, tofu, egg and pork that’s both healthy and addictive. Alongside it sit rafute (melting sweet-soy pork belly), tofu dishes, sea vegetables and pork cooked “from snout to tail.” Hearty, distinctive and deeply local, Okinawan home cooking is a highlight of any visit.

item.title: Sapporo Ramen Guide: Miso Ramen, Best Shops & How to Eat
item.description: Sapporo is the birthplace of miso ramen, one of Japan’s three great ramen styles — and a bowl built for Hokkaido winters. Rich, hearty and warming, it pairs a deep miso-based pork broth with thick, curly yellow noodles, a slick of lard to keep it piping hot, and toppings like sweetcorn, butter, beansprouts and chashu. Slurping a steaming bowl in a tiny counter shop while snow falls outside is a classic Hokkaido moment.

item.title: Sapporo Soup Curry Guide: What It Is & Where to Eat
item.description: Soup curry is a Sapporo original and one of Hokkaido’s most addictive dishes — a fragrant, spiced, brothy curry that’s worlds apart from the thick Japanese curry-rice found elsewhere. A light but deeply flavoured soup, often built on chicken or seafood stock and a blend of spices, comes brimming with big chunks of Hokkaido vegetables — pumpkin, lotus root, peppers, broccoli — and a hero protein like fall-off-the-bone chicken leg. You choose your spice level and eat it by dipping spoonfuls of rice into the soup.

item.title: Sea Grapes (Umibudo) Guide: Okinawa's Seafood & Where to Eat
item.description: Umibudo (“sea grapes”) are one of Okinawa’s most distinctive delicacies — a bright-green sea vegetable of tiny, caviar-like beads that pop with a fresh, briny crunch in the mouth. Rich in minerals and part of the island’s celebrated longevity diet, they’re served cool with a dipping sauce as a refreshing starter. Alongside other sea vegetables like mozuku and a bounty of tropical fish, sea grapes showcase the clean, ocean-forward side of Okinawan cuisine.

item.title: Tsukishima Monja Guide: Tokyo's DIY Griddle Soul Food
item.description: Of all Tokyo’s regional specialities, monjayaki is the one most visitors have never heard of — and the one locals will most enthusiastically send you to try. It’s Tokyo’s own runnier, savoury cousin of Osaka’s okonomiyaki: a loose, dashi-rich batter studded with cabbage and your chosen ingredients, cooked by you on a hot iron griddle built into your table, then scraped up bite by bite with a tiny spatula. It is messy, interactive, deeply local, and genuinely delicious — and the place to eat it is Tsukishima, a small island in the Sumida delta whose Monja Street packs more than 70 monja restaurants into a few atmospheric blocks.
